corrected_value.title: Influence Without Confidence: Upper Chambers and Government Formation

decisions.quote:
The most
L44@P0: sophisticated study to give clear answers to these questions is still that of Druckman, Martin and Thies (2005), which
L45@P0: argues that upper houses influence cabinet formation, regardless of their formal powers. We dispute these answers
L46@P0: theoretically and empirically.
decisions.reason: Both shipped and blind coding (target_index 0) correctly identify Druckman, Martin and Thies (2005), 'Influence without confidence: Upper chambers and government formation' (Legislative Studies Quarterly 30(4): 529-548), as the single original study re-analyzed by this paper. Martin and Stevenson (2001) is cited only as the underlying dataset from which Druckman, Martin and Thies (2005) drew their eight-country sample, not as a finding re-tested here.

decisions.quote:
We were able to
L138@P1: replicate the results of their conditional logit analysis
L139@P1: (DMT’s model 4),3 given in column (2) of Table 1.4 The
L140@P1: statistically significant coefficient of 1.11 implies an odds
L141@P1: ratio of 3.03, which means that majority status in the upper
L142@P1: house triples the chances for a potential government to
L143@P1: form.
decisions.reason: Using the replication files downloaded from the original authors' websites (Note 4, L305@P3), the authors report that they successfully reproduced the original conditional logit analysis (DMT's Model 4 and interaction model, reported under '1:1 Replications' in columns 1 and 2 of Table 1). Both shipped and blind coding correctly classify outcome_computation as 'computationally reproducible'.

decisions.quote:
Closer inspection of the data shows, however, that the
L239@P3: results are not robust. Instead, the evidence suggests that
L240@P3: upper houses do not matter at all, at least in DMT’s sample.
L241@P3: The reason is that the Irish case adds only four government
L242@P3: formations to the analysis (1981, two in 1982, 1987), and
L243@P3: removing those four is sufficient for the coefficient to
L244@P3: become insignificant (column 4).
decisions.reason: In re-analyses of the original eight-country dataset, the authors show that DMT's finding is not robust: restricting to the six countries with symmetric upper houses (column 3), excluding the four Irish formation episodes (column 4), recoding the four Irish cases to reflect Senate composition prior to the new prime minister's nominations (column 5), or estimating a mixed logit model on DMT's dataset (Note 3) all render the effect of upper house majorities statistically insignificant. Both shipped and blind coding correctly record 'robustness challenges'.

decisions.quote:
DMT use the dataset by Martin and Stevenson (2001), but
L118@P1: focus only on the 8 of 14 countries with upper chambers (p.
L119@P1: 535). This is a small basis for drawing general conclusions,
L120@P1: but we stick to the sample for the sake of comparable
L121@P1: results.
decisions.reason: The authors downloaded the replication files from the original authors' websites (L305@P3) and kept the original eight-country sample of 110 cabinet formations to re-run DMT's conditional logit models and perform robustness re-analyses (subsetting cases and recoding the four existing Irish formation opportunities in the sample). Because the study re-analyzes the original study's own dataset and code rather than testing the finding in a new sample, both shipped and blind coding correctly classify the record type as 'reproduction'.
